item.title: The Houthis’ capture of Mocha has transformed the war in Yemen – and the geopolitics of the Red Sea — Chatham House
item.description:
Chatham House · September 14, 2026 · 3 min · Directly readable

Farea Al-Muslimi argues that the Houthi seizure of Mocha and advances along the Bab al-Mandab coast are the most consequential territorial shift in Yemen for years. The move raises the risk of renewed civil war while giving the Houthis greater leverage over shipping through the Red Sea; paired with Iranian pressure around Hormuz, it links two strategic maritime chokepoints. The advance also exposes persistent fragmentation among anti-Houthi forces despite Saudi efforts to coordinate them.

Why it broadens: Connects a local territorial change to global logistics and alliance design. Chokepoint risk is not only about naval capability; it also depends on fragmented partners, commercial ownership networks and who can credibly control coastlines.

item.title: Shrink the UN — Foreign Affairs
item.description:
Foreign Affairs · September 21, 2026 · long · Publisher link; tested source works in Brave

Richard Gowan’s argument for the next UN secretary-general starts from constraint rather than institutional aspiration. Great-power rivalry limits broad diplomatic bargains, donor retrenchment is forcing real budget cuts, and the organization cannot preserve every post–Cold War ambition at equal priority. He argues for a smaller UN centered on a few functions where it retains comparative value: crisis prevention and conflict management, efficient humanitarian response, and achievable development work, while shedding duplicative bureaucracy and lower-value diplomatic process.

Why it broadens: A defense of multilateralism through retrenchment rather than expansion. It asks whether credibility is better preserved by openly narrowing missions than by maintaining mandates that politics and funding no longer support.

Access: If the in-app browser paywalls this, open externally in Brave.

item.title: The Disruptive Politics of AI — Carnegie Endowment for International Peace
item.description:
Carnegie Endowment · September 22, 2026 · long collection · Directly readable

Steve Feldstein and Shreya Joshi introduce a cross-regional collection on AI and political power. Their central point is double-sided: falling inference costs give governments unprecedented scale, speed and efficiency in surveillance, censorship and information control, but the same tools can lower the cost of organizing, documenting abuse and coordinating resistance. The collection ranges from China’s censorship limits and Iran’s wartime internet controls to Thailand’s transnational repression, Asian Gen Z protests, AI sovereignty in India and the UAE, China’s global AI diplomacy and automation bias in military targeting.

Why it broadens: Replaces a one-directional “AI empowers autocrats” story with an institutional one: the political effect of AI depends on state capacity, activist adaptation, infrastructure control and international rule-setting.
